lead: WordNet and FrameNet turn lexical knowledge into reusable networks. WordNet links word senses by semantic relations: car is a hyponym of vehicle. FrameNet links predicate senses to the roles they take: buy evokes a commerce frame with a buyer, goods and seller. Such networks give NLP systems a stable sense inventory, so a program can compare senses, follow IS-A links, or fill role slots without retraining from raw text. They are used in word sense disambiguation, information extraction, question answering, machine translation and multilingual dictionary building.
prereq: You need word senses and lexical relations from Chapter 4.3; sense selection is covered in Chapter 4.5.

blocks.text: WordNet is a lexical database for English. It groups word forms by sense into synsets. A synset is a set of synonymous lemmas that can stand for the same concept in some context. A lemma is a word form as it appears in a synset, such as car or auto. A gloss is the definition attached to a synset, often with an example. The sense inventory is the full set of synsets. A sense number is the index of a lemma's sense, written car#1; it is a listing order, not a promise of corpus frequency. Lexicographer files group synsets by subject, for example noun.artifact, where car synsets sit.

Most pointers link synsets: hypernym, hyponym, meronym, holonym and entailment. Hypernym means IS-A: car → motor vehicle. Hyponym is the reverse. Part meronym means part-of: wheel is a meronym of car. Entailment links a verb sense to an implied activity, as snore entails sleep. Two pointer types, antonym and derivation, link lemmas: hot is the antonym of cold, buy is derivationally related to buyer. The noun hierarchy is rooted at entity. It is a graph because a synset may have several hypernyms.

blocks.where: dist is the number of edges on the shortest path between synset s1 and synset s2.
depth is edges from the root; LCS is the lowest common subsumer; s1 and s2 are synsets.

blocks.text: FrameNet is a lexical database built on frame semantics. A frame is a schematic event or situation with participants and props. A frame element (FE) is a role in that frame. Core FEs define the frame; remove one and the event changes. Peripheral FEs add time, place or purpose but do not define the event. A lexical unit (LU) is a lemma in one sense that evokes a frame, such as buy.v in Commerce_buy.

The sentence “Meera bought a scooter from Ravi for ₹60,000” evokes Commerce_buy. Buyer is Meera, Goods is a scooter, Seller is Ravi, and Money is ₹60,000. Buyer, Goods and Seller are core FEs; Time and Place would be peripheral. Frame elements are close to semantic roles in Chapter 4.6, but FrameNet ties each role to a named frame.

Frames link to frames. Inheritance passes FEs from a general frame to a specific one. Perspective presents the same event from another side: Commerce_buy and Commerce_sell view one exchange from buyer and seller. A subframe is a step inside a larger frame. A synset and a frame are different. A synset groups word forms with the same sense. A frame groups predicates that describe the same event and its roles. One word sense can sit in one synset and evoke one frame, but the two inventories answer different questions.

sections.h3: Indian language wordnets and multilingual dictionaries

blocks.text: An Indian language wordnet, in the IndoWordNet style, treats a synset as an interlingual concept. Each concept has a synset ID, an integer. Every language has its own lemma set, gloss and examples under that ID. Hindi कार and Tamil கார் can carry the same car synset ID while keeping different word forms, scripts and usage notes. English often acts as the pivot language: a new language links to an English synset, and other languages reach it through the same ID.

A multilingual dictionary built this way links senses, not exact translations. Two words may be translation equivalents in one context and differ in another. The synset ID says “same concept”; it does not say “same word in every sentence.” Word sense disambiguation, covered in Chapter 4.5, chooses which synset fits a context.

Metaphor is a short advanced topic; only a few universities teach it. A conceptual metaphor understands one domain through another. ARGUMENT IS WAR appears in “she attacked my position” and “he defended his claim.” The words come from war, but the topic is argument. Metaphor processing is left to advanced courses.

examples.question: In a toy WordNet noun hierarchy the root entity has depth 0. vehicle has depth 1, motor vehicle depth 2, car depth 3, and compact car depth 4. For car and motor vehicle: (a) give the shortest path length in edges, (b) compute path similarity = 1/(dist+1), (c) compute Wu-Palmer = 2 × depth(LCS) / (depth(car) + depth(motor vehicle)). Also (d) write the car synset and name one hypernym and one hyponym, (e) name the relation between car and automobile, (f) name the FrameNet frame for buy and three core FEs, and (g) explain how an Indian language wordnet shares the synset car without sharing the word form.
steps: Depth of car = 3 edges. Depth of motor vehicle = 2 edges.
The lowest common subsumer LCS of car and motor vehicle is motor vehicle. Depth of LCS = 2 edges.
The shortest path is car → motor vehicle. It has dist = 1 edge.
The car#1 noun synset is {car, auto, automobile, motorcar}. One hypernym is motor vehicle; one hyponym is compact car.
car and automobile are synonyms in the same synset. The relation is synonymy.
buy evokes Commerce_buy. Three core FEs are Buyer, Goods and Seller.
An Indian language wordnet gives the car concept one synset ID. Hindi and Tamil entries use their own lemmas under that ID. English can be the pivot. The concept is shared; the word form is not.
examples.answer: The numeric answers are 1 edge, 0.5 and 0.8; the car synset is {car, auto, automobile, motorcar}, its hypernym is motor vehicle, its hyponym is compact car, car and automobile are synonyms, buy evokes Commerce_buy with core FEs Buyer, Goods and Seller, and an Indian wordnet shares the synset ID but not the word form.

traps: A synset is not one word; it is a set of synonymous lemmas. The car synset has several lemmas, so writing only car loses information.
A sense number is a listing index, not a frequency guarantee. car#1 is the first listed noun sense, not always the most frequent sense in your corpus.
Frame elements are not WordNet pointers and not grammatical relations. Buyer in Commerce_buy can be subject or object depending on voice.
A multilingual dictionary links senses, not exact translations. The same synset ID can carry different word forms, scripts and usage notes.
Path similarity uses the shortest path, so direction does not matter for distance. Hypernym direction still matters when you read the graph.

quiz.a: A synset is a set of synonymous lemmas for one sense. A lemma is a word form in a synset. A gloss is the definition and often an example for the synset.

quiz.q: Why is the WordNet noun hierarchy a graph rather than a tree?
quiz.a: A synset may have more than one hypernym, so it can inherit from several parents. A tree allows only one parent. The multiple IS-A links make the structure a directed graph.

quiz.q: In the toy hierarchy entity depth 0, vehicle depth 1, motor vehicle depth 2, car depth 3: compute path similarity and Wu-Palmer for car and vehicle.
quiz.a: Path is car → motor vehicle → vehicle, so dist = 2 edges. Path similarity = 1/(2+1) = 0.333. LCS is vehicle at depth 1. Wu-Palmer = 2×1/(3+1) = 0.5.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between a FrameNet frame element and a WordNet relation, using buy as the example.
quiz.a: A FrameNet frame element is a role inside one event frame, such as Buyer or Goods in Commerce_buy. A WordNet relation is a link between synsets, such as hypernymy between car and motor vehicle. The FE answers who does what in the event; the WordNet pointer answers how two concepts are lexically related.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a core frame element and a peripheral frame element?
quiz.a: A core FE is needed to define the frame and its event. A peripheral FE adds optional information such as Time, Place or Purpose without changing the frame identity.

quiz.q: Label Buyer, Goods, Seller and Money in “Meera bought a scooter from Ravi for ₹60,000” using Commerce_buy.
quiz.a: Buyer = Meera. Goods = scooter. Seller = Ravi. Money = ₹60,000. The predicate bought evokes Commerce_buy.

quiz.q: How can an IndoWordNet-style wordnet share the car synset across Hindi and Tamil without treating the two words as exact translations?
quiz.a: The car concept gets one synset ID. Hindi and Tamil each store their own lemma set, gloss and examples under that ID. English can act as the pivot. The ID links senses, not word strings. Translators still check context, because two words can differ outside the shared sense.

beyond: Not for the exam. WordNet IDs and FrameNet frames appear as features in word sense disambiguation, information extraction and question answering. BabelNet and ConceptNet merge multilingual wordnets with encyclopedic and common-sense links. FrameNet-style frames support event extraction and semantic role labelling. Indic language wordnets support cross-lingual retrieval and translation. Search for IndoWordNet, FrameNet, BabelNet and lexical knowledge graph alignment.
